hints: Follow the arrows in Fig. 6.1 from top to bottom. Blood glucose is above the set point and the final outcome is a decrease, so focus on what type of hormone would lower blood glucose.
Recall the two pancreatic hormones with opposite effects. The one released when glucose is high increases uptake into respiring tissues like fat and skeletal tissue and promotes storage in the liver.
Think about the storage polysaccharide made in liver cells when glucose is plentiful, formed by linking many glucose molecules together.
walkthrough:
Link High Blood Glucose to the Correct Hormone**
After a carbohydrate-rich meal, glucose is absorbed into the blood so concentration rises above the set point. Beta cells in the islets of Langerhans detect this and secrete insulin, so P is insulin. Insulin is the only hormone that lowers blood glucose.

Identify the Target Tissues for Uptake**
Insulin increases the permeability of cell surface membranes to glucose and increases the number of glucose transporter channels, especially in fat cells and skeletal muscle cells that respire a lot of glucose. That makes Q muscle cells.

Name the Storage Product in the Liver**
In liver cells insulin activates enzymes that convert glucose to the storage polysaccharide glycogen. This is glycogenesis, so R is glycogen. Removing glucose from blood to form glycogen helps bring blood glucose down.
Final answer: P - insulin; Q - muscle (liver also accepted for uptake); R - glycogen.

hints: Look at the start and end of Fig. 6.1. The change away from normal triggers a response that reverses that same change back toward normal.
walkthrough:
Recognise Reversal Toward the Set Point**
A rise above the set point is detected and the response - release of P and removal of glucose - causes a decrease back toward the set point. When a deviation triggers the opposite response to restore the norm, that is negative feedback. It keeps blood glucose within narrow limits.

hints: Start by thinking about the opposite situation to Fig. 6.1. If glucose is below the set point, a different pancreatic cell type releases the hormone that raises blood glucose.
Remember that this hormone is a protein that cannot cross the cell surface membrane, so focus on where it binds on a liver cell and what membrane protein it first activates.
Think about the enzyme in the membrane that makes a small cyclic molecule from ATP once the first transducer is active.
Consider why that small molecule is called a second messenger and what it does inside the cytoplasm to a series of enzymes.
Recall that enzymes in this pathway are switched on by addition of phosphate and that one molecule at the start can activate many molecules downstream.
Link the final activated enzymes to the breakdown of the storage polysaccharide you named in (a)(i) into glucose.
Remember there is a second way the liver makes new glucose from non-carbohydrates to add to the blood, as well as release of glucose into the blood.
walkthrough:
Name the Hormone for Low Blood Glucose**
When blood glucose falls below the set point, alpha cells in the islets of Langerhans secrete glucagon. Glucagon is the antagonist to insulin and its target is mainly liver cells.

Binding at the Liver Cell Surface**
Glucagon is a peptide hormone so it is hydrophilic and cannot diffuse through the phospholipid bilayer. It binds to a specific complementary receptor on the cell surface membrane of a liver cell. This activates a G-protein inside the membrane.

Formation of the Second Messenger**
The activated G-protein activates the enzyme adenyl cyclase in the membrane. Adenyl cyclase converts ATP to cyclic AMP, known as cAMP. cAMP is the second messenger because glucagon is the first messenger that never enters the cell.

Enzyme Cascade and Amplification**
 cAMP activates protein kinases which activate further enzymes in sequence. This is an enzyme cascade. Each enzyme activates many molecules of the next enzyme, so the signal is amplified. Activation is by phosphorylation, using phosphate from ATP.

Glycogen Breakdown to Glucose**
The final enzymes break down glycogen to glucose. This is glycogenolysis. Because of amplification, a small amount of glucagon causes breakdown of a large amount of glycogen very quickly.

Making New Glucose and Raising Blood Glucose**
Liver cells also carry out gluconeogenesis, formation of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources such as amino acids and glycerol. Glucose is then transported out of liver cells into the blood, raising blood glucose concentration back up to the set point.

Final answer: Hormone is glucagon. Glucagon binds to receptors on liver cell surface membrane, activating G-protein then adenyl cyclase which converts ATP to cAMP (second messenger). cAMP triggers an enzyme cascade with activation by phosphorylation and amplification. This causes glycogenolysis to glucose and gluconeogenesis, glucose released into blood, returning concentration to set point.
